title: Almost half
hook: a diary study found that a little under half of daily actions were habits (Wood et al.)

segments.voice: Yesterday, trainable: attention can grow, modestly and really. That closed the attention stretch. Did you give one return a quiet nod? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-four.

Which hand held the toothbrush this morning? Which shoe went on first? Which way did you turn at the end of the street, and did you decide to, or did your feet just go? Most of those questions are hard to answer, and that's the interesting part. A lot of a day happens without anyone choosing it. A new stretch of the path starts here: habit. The attention days asked where the mind goes. The habit days ask what the body and the day do while the mind is somewhere else. And the first finding is a simple, startling fraction.
screen: `WHICH SHOE WENT ON FIRST?` → `NOBODY CHOSE IT.` → `A NEW STRETCH: HABIT.`

segments.voice: First, the diary. Psychologist Wendy Wood and her colleagues asked people to stop at regular times through the day and write down what they were doing, thinking and feeling. Not a survey about habits. Just a running log of ordinary life. Second, how they spotted a habit. The researchers looked for actions done nearly every day, and usually in the same place. Brushing teeth in the same bathroom. Checking the same screen at the same desk. Third, the fraction. When they added it up, a little under half of what people did in a day fit that pattern. Almost half. Not most of life, but close enough to half to make anyone look twice at an ordinary day. Fourth, where the mind went. During those habits, people often reported thinking about something else entirely. The hands ran the routine; the mind was off planning, worrying, replaying. So almost half of a day may be running on tracks laid down earlier. That can sound like bad news. It can also be good news, because tracks can be laid on purpose. Long before any diary study, the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote in his Meditations: "Such as are thy habitual thoughts, such also will be the character of thy mind; for the soul is dyed by the thoughts." Dyed, like cloth soaking in a vat, a little deeper each time. The science measured actions; Marcus was writing about thoughts. Both point at the same quiet power of repetition.
screen: `AN ORDINARY DAY, WRITTEN DOWN.` · `SAME THING, SAME PLACE.` · then, large: `A LITTLE UNDER HALF.` · then: `THE MIND ELSEWHERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: three habits from today. Sit, and let the breath settle for a few rounds. Then walk back through the day so far, slowly, like rewinding a video. Find three things you did without deciding to do them: the way you made the coffee, the route you took, the first app you opened. Name each one quietly. No judgment, good habit or bad. Just see them. Then let them go, and rest on the breath, which runs all day without any deciding at all. The bell holds the time.
Almost half. In a diary study, a little under half of what people did each day were habits, done in the same place, often with the mind elsewhere. Today's word.
Your line: almost half. Today, catch one habit in the act, mid-motion, and notice for one breath where your mind was while your hands were busy. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: People who study their own habits sometimes keep a simple log for a day, noting what they do and where, to see how much of the day runs on routine; contemplatives in several traditions treat repeated thoughts and acts as what slowly shapes a life.

trapdoor: what you thought: most of a day is made of choices.
what it means: in the diary study, almost half of what people did were habits, run with the mind elsewhere.
what a scholar hears: habit is defined here by repetition and setting, not by how it feels, which is why place matters so much in the research that followed.
